Where it began

Andrew Symonds was born in Birmingham on 9 June 1975 and moved to Australia as a toddler. He grew up first in Charters Towers in northern Queensland, where his junior cricket meant long drives to Townsville, and then on the Gold Coast. He was only 15 when he first played grade cricket for the Gold Coast Dolphins, and he celebrated with a double hundred.

As a young man he could have played for England, the land of his birth. After a first season with Gloucestershire in 1995 he was picked for an England A tour, but he turned it down. He wanted to play for Australia.

The player

He was a powerful right-handed batsman in the middle order who could bowl both medium pace and off-spin. One-day cricket made his name. At the 2003 World Cup he hit an unbeaten 143 against Pakistan after Australia had lost four early wickets, and in five innings at that tournament he was out only twice. Four years later he was part of the side that won the World Cup again.

In Tests he played 26 matches between 2004 and 2008, making 1,462 runs at 40.61 and taking 24 wickets. His first Test hundred came in front of a Boxing Day crowd at Melbourne in 2006, when he came in at 5 for 84 and made 156, reaching three figures with a six. At Sydney in January 2008 he went one better, with 162 not out.

What made him special

Ricky Ponting rated him the best fielder he had ever seen. Tall and strong but quick on his feet, he could cover huge amounts of ground, hold anything near him and throw down the stumps from the deep. With the bat he simply hit the ball very hard. Playing for Gloucestershire against Glamorgan in 1995 he struck 16 sixes in an innings of 254 not out, a first-class record at the time, and for Kent in 2004 he reached a Twenty20 hundred in 34 balls.

Test cricket asked a little more patience of him than the one-day game did, and he took a while to find his feet. Once he settled, he showed what he could do.

Away from the middle

Everyone called him Roy. An early coach thought he looked like the Brisbane basketball player Leroy Loggins, and the shortened name stuck for life. He was a lifelong Brisbane Broncos fan, once trained with them, and turned out in a rugby league game for Wynnum Manly. He loved fishing, made a cameo in a Bollywood film and later commentated on the Big Bash.

Kent supporters voted him their greatest overseas white-ball player in 2020. He died in 2022, aged 46.

And finally

In the 2007 World Cup final, played in near darkness after the rain, it was Symonds who bowled the very last ball. Most players would be happy just to catch the winning moment. He preferred to deliver it.
